title: Sonnet 97 and the absence sonnets
short: This is the first of three sonnets (97-99) on being away from the beloved, in which the images of the seasons measure the speaker's loss.
body: Sonnets 97-99 share the theme of separation and the language of seasons and flowers; Sonnet 98 begins 'From you have I been absent in the spring'. The argument of 97 is a paradox. The absence actually fell in summer and autumn, yet it felt like winter. 'How like' opens an exclamation, not a question. The sonnet's three quatrains move from winter (ll. 1-4) to the actual summer and autumn (ll. 5-10) and to the silence of the birds (ll. 11-12), so the year is gone through twice, once as feeling and once as fact.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: absence
short: The speaker is the one who has been away: 'my absence ... From thee' makes him the one who left, not the beloved.
body: Editors point out that the absence is his own, though 'thou away' (l. 12) later reverses the point of view. Running the sentence on from 'been' to 'From thee' stresses the separation. Absence as winter is an old figure, but Shakespeare's version makes the beloved the source of the year's 'pleasure'. The paradox that the traveller, not the stay-at-home, feels the winter is part of the poem's wit.

anchor: the pleasure of the fleeting year
title: fleeting year
short: The beloved is the delight of the fast-passing year. 'Fleeting' contrasts with the winter that seemed to have no end.
body: The phrase makes the beloved the joy that gives the year its meaning; without him the year is only time going by. The quickness of 'fleeting' is set against the speaker's slow 'freezings' and 'dark days'. The year passes quickly because time is short and beauty fades, a theme of the earlier sonnets. Here, though, the speed is set against the speaker's experience, for whom the time of absence dragged like a long winter. The paradox of a year that is both fleeting and endless prepares for the clash between the actual season and the felt one in ll. 5-10.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: Old December
short: December is personified as an old man at the end of the year. Its 'bareness' is the stripped trees and fields.
body: The year was often pictured as a human life, with December as old age (compare The Winter's Tale 4.4). 'Bareness' suggests both the leafless season and poverty. The three exclamations of ll. 3-4 build up the picture of winter before the turn at 'And yet' (l. 5). The word 'everywhere' extends the private winter to the whole world. The bare month is the opposite of the 'teeming autumn' that follows.

sources.cite: John Kerrigan, ed., The Sonnets and A Lover's Complaint (Penguin, 1986), commentary

title: time removed
short: 'This time removed' is the period of separation: the time when he was removed from the beloved, and also a time now past.
body: Booth notes both senses: the time when I was away, and a time at a distance from now. 'Was summer's time' corrects the opening simile, because it really was summer, though it felt like winter. As editors observe, the season meant runs from late summer into autumn, the time of harvest. So the line marks the turn from the felt season to the real one.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: Teeming autumn
short: Autumn is pregnant ('teeming', 'big') with its harvest, the 'increase' or produce of the land.
body: 'Teem' means to bear offspring in abundance, and 'big' means pregnant. 'Increase' is the Bible's word for the crops of the land (Leviticus 26:4, 'the land shall yield her increase'). The early procreation sonnets use the same vocabulary ('From fairest creatures we desire increase', Sonnet 1). The image of the fruitful season, normally a sign of joy, is preparing to turn into mourning in l. 8.

anchor: the wanton burden of the prime
title: The wanton burden of the prime
short: Autumn carries the fruit conceived in the playful, lustful spring ('prime'), like a mother carrying a child of spring's love-play.
body: 'Wanton' means playful, luxuriant and sexually free. A 'burden' is what is carried, here a child in the womb; the word could also mean a song's refrain, a possible second sense. 'Prime' is spring. The image tells the seasons as a story: conception in spring, birth in autumn. The joining of fertility and wantonness also recalls the sexual energy of the procreation sonnets.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: Widowed wombs
short: Autumn is like a widow pregnant with her dead husband's child: fruitful but in mourning, because the father (summer) is gone.
body: The simile makes the harvest sad. The crops are children born after their father has died. 'Lords' means husbands, with a hint of aristocratic widowhood. The father is summer, who 'waits on' the absent beloved (l. 11), so the fruit is fatherless. Posthumous children were a familiar fact of early modern life. The image brings together the poem's two worlds, nature's harvest and human grief, and makes autumn's very abundance a sign of loss.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: Hope of orphans
short: To him the harvest seemed only the prospect of orphans, children born with no father to provide for them.
body: 'Hope of orphans' can mean orphans still to come, or the only hope that orphans have, which is a bleak inheritance. A child who had lost one parent could be called an orphan. 'Unfather'd fruit' joins the plant and human senses of 'fruit', as in 'the fruit of the womb' (Psalm 127:3). 'Abundant issue' in l. 9 means a plentiful crop or progeny, with 'issue' a legal word for heirs.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: Summer waits on thee
short: Summer is personified as a servant who attends the beloved, so wherever he is, it is summer. 'His' means 'its'.
body: 'Wait on' means serve and attend, and also wait for. The idea that the beloved makes the season reverses nature, since the year's warmth follows him rather than the calendar. The beloved has become the season's lord, almost a god of plenty like Bacchus, whom summer serves. Since summer and its pleasures have followed him, the land the speaker sees has its fruit but none of its delight, which explains why the harvest seemed to him only orphaned. The line gives the reason ('For') for the whole paradox of ll. 5-10.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: Mute birds
short: With the beloved gone, even the birds stop singing. The fiction also fits autumn, when few birds sing.
body: 'Thou away' is an absolute construction meaning 'you being away'. The birds' silence attributes human grief to nature, but it is also a fact of late summer (compare Sonnet 102: 'As Philomel in summer's front doth sing ... But that wild music burthens every bough'). The couplet then allows that the birds may sing, though sadly. The silence of the birds was a convention for grief.

title: cheer
short: 'Cheer' first meant face or expression and then mood. The birds sing so gloomily that the leaves turn pale.
body: The word comes from Old French chiere ('face'), and in Shakespeare's time it could still mean a person's look as well as their mood. In the last line the leaves 'look pale', as if from fear, at the approach of winter, so their autumn yellowing becomes dread. The ending returns to the winter of l. 1, now no longer a metaphor but a season on its way.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
